lines.say: Here's a puzzle. A gate secretly turns a special state by a fraction of a turn.
That fraction is its phase, and in chemistry, it's the number we're after.
To read it, picture a clock hand moving the same secret amount every tick.
Photograph it after one, two and four ticks. The four tick photo magnifies tiny differences.
Phase estimation takes these photos with counting qubits. Call the gate U, and its fraction phi.
Each counting qubit starts in ket plus, an even mix of zero and one, and controls U.
Phase kickback, from lesson fifteen, moves the turn onto that qubit's hand.
Run U once, and the first hand turns phi. Run it twice, two phi, and four times, four phi.
Doubling slides phi's binary digits, its zeros and ones, one place left, and whole turns vanish, so each hand shows a finer digit.
Try the S gate, which turns ket one a quarter turn, zero point zero one in binary.
With two counting qubits, one hand turns a quarter, the other a half.
Here the picture breaks: measuring a qubit gives zero or one, never its hand.
Instead, the inverse Q F T from lesson eighteen combines the hands into the digits zero one.
The input must be a state U only turns, called an eigenstate, like ket one for S.
Hand it any other state, and you get a random one of U's phases.
So kick U, U twice and U four times onto counting qubits, and the inverse Q F T reads phi's binary digits.
